newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB officials may quit in Japan racketeer scandal.
newsitem.headline: DKB officials may quit in Japan racketeer scandal.

text.p: Top executives at leading Japanese commercial bank Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) were under pressure on Wednesday to resign in the latest chapter in a scandal over links between racketeers and financial firms.

The Japanese business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda and president Katsuhiko Kondo were expected to resign to take "social" and "moral" responsibility for DKB's huge loans to a racketeer accused of taking illegal payoffs from Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
Kuniji Miyazaki, currently an adviser to the bank and president when the loans were made in the 1980s, would also resign, it said.
Media reports have said the racketeer used the loans to buy shares in Nomura Securities.
A DKB spokesman told Reuters no decision had been made on any executive changes.
Meanwhile, prosecutors staged more raids on DKB in connection with its investigation into the scandal over payoffs to the racketeer, Ryuichi Koike.
DKB has said it regrets the raids on its offices but has said it cannot comment on loans to individual clients.

Japan's Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings. They gain access to the meetings by buying stakes in the companies.
Analysts said DKB itself may have violated the code or have committed a breach of trust if it extended loans without collateral to the racketeer.
They said the image of DKB, Japan's third-biggest commercial bank, had been severely tainted by the reports of links to the racketeer.
"DKB's top management will be forced to take responsibility for its involvement in the scandal," said Yushiro Ikuyo, first vice president at Smith Barney International Inc.

A financial industry source said if president Kondo resigned, it could have a major impact on DKB's future as he is a key figure in DKB's plans for Japan's "Big Bang" deregulation of financial markets.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori were arrested last week on suspicion of taking some 50 million yen ($442,000) in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
On Wednesday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the ministry was ready to take strict action against DKB when the bank's role in the scandal was determined.

"The impact of this case on the overall financial industry is by no means small," Mitsuzuka said. "It (the ministry) may take strict measures when the overall picture of the investigation becomes clear."
However, analysts said that the impact of any penalties on DKB would be limited.
The Finance Ministry is likely to issue an order to DKB to improve its business practices, but the punishment would not be on the same scale as the expected action against Nomura, they said.
"DKB's share price will be under pressure for a while. But the incident will not have a direct impact on its business performance," one analyst said. ($1=113 yen)
